<reason>The debate narrowed to three clashes: (1) scope of "such as MBTI and DISC," (2) whether the team-building half needs predictive validity, and (3) the real-world counterfactual. CON's scoping gambit — that the motion sweeps in Big Five instruments PRO conceded predict — was its cleanest structural play, but PRO answered it squarely and early: the motion's stated reason scopes its target, so predictive instruments are not in the crosshairs. That answer largely defused CON's central lever and made CON's remaining position legalistic rather than substantive. PRO's Q1 then forced the decisive admission: CON advised keeping the tools while treating the letter as "a headline you can ignore." PRO's exploitation of that ("nobody buys DISC for the intensity graph; the workshop is named after the letters") was the sharpest weighing in the debate, and CON's abolition-versus-correction rejoinder, while genuinely live, never showed that employers actually use the continuous scales rather than the codes. On team-building, PRO's "prediction wearing a friendlier hat" plus the truth bar ("something false, in writing, with a logo," sticky through staffing and promotion) beat CON's scaffold defence, and PRO's counterfactual point that tests sit on top of the unstructured chat rather than replacing it blunted CON's "structure versus gut feel" frame. PRO also handled CON's vendor-inconsistency pressure cleanly (admission against interest versus advertising). CON's contestable-score reply and its point that firms actually buy questionnaires while refusing free structure kept it competitive, but two of CON's turns were clipped for overlength — a real execution cost, including a truncated Rebuttal 2 tally. PRO made the decision easier and left fewer live burdens.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 and the follow-up: forcing CON to say whether it would tell a firm to keep scoring by MBTI type or DISC quadrant. CON's answer — keep them but ignore the letter — was then framed as "a defence of some other product hiding inside their packaging," which reduced CON's case to a complaint about a headline while PRO's harm (a sticky, flippable, logoed label) remained intact.</best_rebuttal>
